2. Motivation

Corporate Facilities Management (CFM) and its sister company A-One clean offices, clinics, plants, churches and government buildings across Alabama. Every new account starts the same way: a supervisor walks the building and takes photos, then a sales manager turns those photos into a price. Between March and November 2026 our sales manager emailed me 45 bid emails containing 90 "Bid Cal" spreadsheets. That is the workload this app is for.

How it is done today. Photos arrive by email (one email per room for a big building). The estimator guesses the square footage, decides how many cleaners and hours a night, fills in an Excel "Job Investment Report", writes a Word proposal, and sends it to me to approve. By my own estimate as the owner this takes half a day or more of estimator time per bid, and the client usually gets the proposal 3 to 5 days after the walkthrough. In commercial cleaning the first credible proposal often wins.

What it costs. Time is the obvious cost. The hidden cost is pricing errors. When I read all 90 spreadsheets for this project I found three patterns that lose money on accounts we win:

  1. A month is priced as 4 weeks. The spreadsheet computes monthly labor as crew × hours × days × 4. A month averages 4.33 weeks, so every recurring bid under-counts labor by about 7.7%. On one $2,102/month account that is roughly $90 of wages a month we pay but never priced.
  2. Workers' comp is never charged. The spreadsheet has a workers' comp line (and a liability line), but in all 90 files the rate applied is 0%. Our real rate is 1.69% of payroll.
  3. The markup is inconsistent. Profit on regular nightly cleaning ranges from 6% to 100% (median 40%) between similar buildings, because each bid is hand-tuned.

Why care: janitorial is a thin-margin, labor-heavy business. A few points of mispriced labor on every account is the difference between a profitable contract and one we clean at a loss for three years.

3. What is new here

I looked at what a cleaning company can buy today. The market splits into calculators that make you type everything, and photo-to-quote apps that price from market averages.

ProductWhat it doesWhat it does not do (that Bid Builder does)
CleanGuru, BidLoom, Janitorial ManagerJanitorial bid calculators built on ISSA production rates; you type in square footage and room counts.Nothing reads the walkthrough. No photo analysis, no proposal writing, no check against the company's own past bids.
QuoteIQ AI EstimatorPhoto-to-quote: up to 5 property photos to a price, ZIP-code calibrated, inside a field-service CRM.Prices from market averages, not the company's own payroll taxes, workers' comp, wage and markup. 5 photos vs. a 49-photo commercial walkthrough. No manager approval gate.
CleanQuote AI, SnapScope, HandoffCustomers or contractors upload photos; AI builds line items or job records.Mostly residential or construction. Not built around nightly janitorial labor math or floor care.
ChatGPT with photosCan describe rooms and guess a price.Does arithmetic in the model (unreliable), no fixed rate card, no injection screening, no audit trail, no budget caps, nothing saved.
CFM today: Excel Bid Cal + Word proposalA sales manager fills a 'Job Investment Report' spreadsheet and writes a Word proposal.Half a day or more per bid, 3 to 5 days to the client. Labor counted on 4-week months; workers' comp never applied; profit varies 6% to 100%.

What is different. (1) It starts from the photos our people already take, up to 60 per bid, and reads room type, floor type, soil level and fixtures from each. (2) It prices with our numbers: $13 starting wage adjustable per job, real 2026 payroll taxes (FICA, FUTA, Alabama SUTA 2.7%), our workers' comp rate 1.69%, supplies 5% of price, equipment 3% (the median of our own spreadsheets), liability 0.05%, and our floor-care prices ($1.25/sq ft strip and wax, $0.85 carpet). (3) The AI never does the arithmetic. Code does, so the price is repeatable and auditable. (4) It checks itself against our real past bids. (5) A manager must approve, and it is hardened against prompt injection. Honest caveat: QuoteIQ's AI Estimator is the closest product; we differ by using the company's own cost structure and past bids, handling large commercial walkthroughs, and keeping a human approval gate.

4. The agents

Five AI agents and three code components. Agents do what language models are good at: looking at photos, grouping messy information, writing, and turning a plain-English request into a precise change. Code does everything that must be exact.

Blue = AI agent (gpt-6-luna) · gray = plain Python code · amber = a person. Arrows show who hands work to whom.

AgentJobToolsOutput (validated by Pydantic)
1 Site SurveyLooks at one photo: room type, floor, soil, visible fixtures, periodic work needed. Copies any text it sees into a quarantined field.none (vision)PhotoSurvey
2 TakeoffGroups photos into areas by room name, estimates square footage, uses the largest fixture count seen, suggests floor care, lists assumptions and questions.list_area_types, get_production_rateTakeoff
3 Proposal WriterCover letter, scope of work, exclusions. Never writes prices.noneProposal
4 RevisionTurns a manager's request into tool calls.get_bid, set_visits_per_week, set_hourly_wage, set_area_sq_ft, add_area, remove_area, add_floor_care, remove_floor_care, set_floor_care_priceRevisionResult
5 Past-Bid ComparisonChooses which real CFM bids are comparable and explains the verdict.list_past_bids, compare_to_past_bidBenchmarkReport

Model. All five agents use gpt-6-luna. Through Nov 18 it ran through Portkey on the Yale course key (the only model allowed on it). That key expired on Nov 21, so the Nov 23 runs use the same model on CFM's own OpenAI key (the course allows a personal OPENAI_API_KEY; the app picks whichever key is present). It reads photos, returns structured output reliably, and at $0.10 / $0.50 per million input/output tokens a whole bid costs well under a cent. Accuracy comes from the design (code for math, a fixed rate card, a checker, a human gate), not from a bigger model.

One real run, step by step: Client E, a manufacturing plant (24 photos)

This is a real live run from 2026-11-23. Photos from a CFM supervisor's walkthrough; the client's name is replaced.

  1. Intake. The estimator picks the saved walkthrough (24 photos, 12 rooms), sets service type, visits and wage. Photos are shrunk to at most 1,568 px; notes are screened for injection (none found).
  2. Site Survey agent, 24 calls, 4 at a time. Each photo becomes a structured record. Signs it read ("Coca-Cola; KEEP OUT") are kept as quarantined text, never acted on.
  3. Takeoff agent, 1 call. The estimator table already held my reviewed size for each of the 10 inside areas, and the agent kept every one of them. It added the two photographed areas I had left out (production aisle and gazebo) as provisional, suggested strip and wax for two VCT floors, and asked: "Please confirm whether the production aisle/walkway and exterior gazebo/sidewalk are in scope."
  4. Pricing engine and Bid Checker (code). Hours per visit = sq ft ÷ ISSA speed × floor and soil factors + fixture minutes, × 1.10 for setup and travel. Then labor, payroll taxes, workers' comp, overhead, supplies, profit. The checker flagged every photo-estimated size, and after the revision it raised a STOP: $0.63/sq ft/month is above the $0.50 ceiling, because this plant is mostly restrooms.
  5. Proposal Writer, 1 call: cover letter, scope by area type, exclusions. Code inserts every number.
  6. Revision agent. I typed: "Drop the outdoor gazebo and the production aisle from the scope, and make it 6 nights a week at $14 an hour.". The agent made 5 tool calls (4 changes); code re-priced; first-year value $42,506.24 → $52,570.85; the bid went back to draft.
  7. Manager approval. The bid stays a draft (watermarked proposal) until a manager approves it.

AI cost is not the constraint. For CFM (a handful of estimators) it is pennies a month. Even 10,000 estimators would cost less than one part-time cleaner.

What we did to keep cost down, and whether it hurt

  • Code does the math. No tokens spent on arithmetic, and no wrong arithmetic. No downside.
  • Photos shrunk to 1,568 px (JPEG q82, EXIF rotation kept). Phone photos arrive at 3 to 12 MB. This cut Site Survey input tokens by 85% in the A/B test below. It did cost some fine detail (see the test).
  • Prompt caching with a cache key per agent. It worked for the Takeoff, Revision and Comparison agents (about 35% of Takeoff input cached on average, when the same prompt ran again within minutes) but did not work for the Site Survey agent: 0 cached tokens on all 247 photo calls, because its shared prompt is shorter than the provider's minimum cacheable prefix. That is an honest miss and the first fix to make.
  • One small call per photo, 4 in parallel instead of one huge call: a failed photo costs one retry, not the whole bid, and model time for 49 photos was 193 s.
  • Hard caps per agent, per bid and per day (Section 6).

What it shows. Shrinking cut input tokens by 85%, cost by 79% and upload size from 34 MB to 1.7 MB, and model time fell from 58 s to 32 s. The answers that drive the price (room type, floor type, soil) stayed the same on 7 of 8 photos each, and on the one room-type change the shrunk photo was the better answer (a public toilet called "restroom" instead of "other"). It did hurt fine detail: the full-size photos read three small signs the shrunk ones missed ("No Smoking", an EXIT sign, a product label), counted 12 desks where the shrunk photo saw 6, and fixture counts differed on 3 of 8 photos. Square footage comes from the estimator's table, not the photos, so the price impact is small. Desk and fixture counts feed restroom and office time, so the next step is to send full-size crops when a photo is dense with fixtures, or let the estimator type counts for big restrooms.

Defenses caught working

Tests. 34 automated tests (pytest) cover pricing by hand, payroll taxes, floor care, injection screening, budget caps, the full pipeline with a fake model, approval rules, revision safety, comparison math, the what-if math and the bad-key message. All 34 pass.

Price quality: tested against 13 real CFM bids

I rebuilt 13 real bids (names removed) in the app's pricing engine, each building as one area type, 5 nights, CFM's own wage, and the app's 15% profit. The app came in a median +11% from CFM's price while counting a median +19% more labor hours. On the outpatient surgical clinic (7,091 sq ft, one cleaner 5 to 9 pm) the app priced $2,126 vs CFM's $2,102 (+1%).

The Past-Bid Comparison agent puts this kind of check in front of the manager on every bid:

Money found in the current process

From reading the 90 spreadsheets: the 4-week month under-prices labor by 7.7%, and workers' comp (1.69%) is left out. Together that is about 9% of labor on every recurring account. On a typical $2,000/month account with about $1,200 of labor, that is roughly $110 a month, $1,300 a year, per account. The app prices both correctly by default.

The what-if chart: a manager's pricing tool

Real user trial (Nov 23, 2026)

At 2:44 PM I emailed a public link to four CFM staff with a 5:00 PM deadline and asked each to run a real bid, time it, and say honestly what was wrong.

TesterWhat happened
Executive administrative assistantRan a real bid on CFM's own office: 15 phone photos, no known sizes, 3 visits a week. The app priced it at $305.50/month janitorial (23 model requests, AI cost $0.0097). It took her 58 minutes in the app on first use (including two change requests), plus a 45-minute walkthrough.
Sales manager and a supervisorCould not get past Build bid ("Failed to fetch"). The tunnel log shows the free public link dropped at 4:31 PM and never reconnected; their attempts came after. A hosting failure, not the agents, but a real one.
Second supervisorNo reply by the deadline.
Her verdict: "the application provides a useful starting point for preparing bids, but the calculations and correction process need further testing before client use." She would not approve the pricing until the issues below are fixed.

What she found, and she is right: (1) Duplicate rooms. Three photos of one conference room became three rooms (350, 300 and 320 sq ft); her tape measure says 304. The same happened in reception and the copy room (135 sq ft measured). The Takeoff agent only groups photos that share a "room__" file-name prefix, and her phone named them IMG_1177 and so on. (2) Floor care: it suggested VCT strip and wax for a ceramic-tile restroom; the Revision agent removed it when she asked. (3) Revisions: asked to merge the conference rooms, the Revision agent asked which of the three sizes to keep instead of guessing, so the price did not change; a later try failed when the link dropped. (4) The "Send back" confirmation was not clear enough. The safety rails held: her flagged draft was never approved, so nothing wrong could reach a client. There is still no timed side-by-side with the Excel process; that is the next test.

8. Limits and next steps

  • Square footage from photos is the weakest link. The AI and a human reviewer can disagree a lot. On Nov 18, with no sizes given, the Takeoff agent put Client E's inside areas at 4,900 sq ft; my own review of the same 24 photos came to 6,950. The app flags every photo-estimated area, and a tape-measured or floor-plan number always overrides it.
  • The site survey prompt is too short to be cached. Cached input was 0 on all 247 photo calls; only the Takeoff agent benefited (about 35% of its input cached on average). A longer shared prefix (the rate card and the area types) would make the survey cacheable.
  • Revisions do not rewrite the cover letter. After the Client E revision, the price and scope table changed but the letter still said five nights. Next: re-run the Proposal Writer after a revision.
  • Several photos of one room become several rooms unless the file names share a "room__" prefix (found by the real user trial). Next: have the Takeoff agent group photos by what it sees, ask the estimator to confirm, and give the Revision agent a "merge areas" tool.
  • Hosting and timing. The free tunnel dropped during the user trial; next is a small always-on server. There is still no timed side-by-side with the Excel process.
  • The Yale course key expired on Nov 21 (Portkey shows "Expired"). The app now accepts either key and says plainly when a key is rejected; the Nov 23 runs used CFM's own OpenAI key.

Next month

  1. Phone-first walkthrough: snap photos room by room in the app instead of emailing them.
  2. Learn CFM's own speeds: compare the app's labor hours with the hours crews actually log on each account and adjust the rate card per building type.
  3. Good / better / best options (how our sales manager already sells) generated from one walkthrough.
  4. Write the approved proposal straight into CFM's Word template and email it from Zoho after approval.
  5. Put it online for the sales team, with logins and one shared bid history.
